title: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM MOSES’ EXCUSES
paragraphs: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM MOSES’ EXCUSES
Some of the greatest tragedies in human history have not come from rebellion.
Not from people running away from God.
But from people standing in front of His calling while quietly whispering reasons why they could never do it.
Most believers know Moses as the man who split the sea, confronted Pharaoh, and led Israel toward freedom.
Few remember that before he became a deliverer, he became an expert at making excuses.
And if we're honest, many of us know exactly how that feels.
We tell ourselves we're waiting for the right moment.
The right level of spiritual maturity.
Yet somewhere beneath those reasons is often the same fear that gripped Moses standing before a burning bush in the wilderness.
A fear that still keeps countless believers from stepping into the story God is writing.
The dreams of his youth seem buried beneath decades of disappointment.
He had once believed he could help deliver his people.
And from that fire came the voice of God.
The Hebrew text records God's declaration:
The phrase carries layers of meaning that are difficult to fully express in English.
It speaks of God's eternal self-existence, His unchanging nature, His sovereignty, and His complete independence from anything outside Himself.
"I am the One who depends on nothing and no one."
The irony is impossible to miss.
The self-sufficient God was calling an insecure man.
And Moses immediately began listing reasons why God had chosen the wrong person.
The first battle was not external.
God places a burden on your heart.
A conversation you need to have.
Who am I to do this?
Who am I to make a difference?
Moses looked at himself and saw weakness.
God looked at Moses and saw purpose.
God never answered Moses by boosting his self-esteem.
God's answer was not confidence in Moses.
It was confidence in God's presence.
Biblical faith has never been self-confidence.
"What if they ask who sent me?"
Again, many believers understand this fear.
What if someone asks a question I cannot answer?
What if I don't know enough Scripture?
What if I cannot explain everything perfectly?
Yet throughout Scripture God repeatedly uses people who do not know everything.
He uses those willing to trust the One who does.
The issue was never Moses' expertise.
"What if they do not believe me?"
Now the fear becomes painfully relatable.
Not because God did not call.
But because people cannot bear the possibility of rejection.
Yet God gave Moses signs to confirm His message.
The miracle was never intended to draw attention to Moses.
It pointed people back to God.
Authentic ministry still works this way.
Whenever ministry becomes centered on personalities, platforms, and personal fame, something has gone terribly wrong.
"I am not a man of words."
Moses believed his weakness disqualified him.
The Creator of speech was not intimidated by Moses' limitations.
And perhaps that is exactly what some believers need to hear today.
The weakness you think disqualifies you may be the very thing God intends to use for His glory.
Because when success comes through obvious weakness, everyone knows where the power originated.
The one beneath all the others.
And what remains is raw reluctance.
Moses simply did not want to go.
That moment may be one of the most relatable passages in all of Scripture.
Because eventually every excuse reaches the same destination.
Fear of what obedience might cost.
Fear of what life looks like when control is handed over to God.
Yet this is where the Gospel begins to shine.
Because Moses' story is not ultimately about excuses.
God knew every objection before Moses ever spoke.
Because centuries later another Deliverer would come.
Unlike Moses, Jesus offered no excuses.
When the Father sent Him into a broken world, He did not hesitate.
The Greek text of Luke 22:42 records Jesus praying:
"μὴ τὸ θέλημά μου, ἀλλὰ τὸ σὸν γινέσθω"
Mē to thelēma mou, alla to son ginesthō.
"Not my will, but Yours be done."
Where Moses hesitated, Christ obeyed perfectly.
Where Moses feared inadequacy, Christ demonstrated perfect faithfulness.
Where Moses needed grace, Jesus became grace incarnate.
The Gospel is not the story of strong people doing extraordinary things.
It is the story of a perfect Savior redeeming weak people who could never save themselves.
This is why Moses' life matters so deeply.
His story proves that God does not wait for perfect people.
The Bible never hides Moses' failures.
Grace takes the scandal of our weakness and turns it into a testimony of God's faithfulness.
Grace takes broken chapters and writes redemption across the pages.
Grace takes ordinary people and places them inside extraordinary purposes.
But Moses once said similar things.
Maybe the greatest lesson Moses teaches us is this:
God's calling was never dependent on Moses' perfection.
And God's calling on your life is not dependent on yours.
The Kingdom of God has always advanced through flawed people surrendered to a perfect Savior.
The question is not whether you have excuses.
The question is whether your excuses will have the final word.
What excuse have you been giving God lately?
Those conversations matter because testimonies strengthen faith and remind struggling believers they are not fighting alone.
Your support helps spread biblical truth, create more Gospel-centered resources, and reach people who desperately need hope in Christ.
Because sometimes the biggest obstacle between us and God's purpose is not our weakness.
It's our refusal to believe that His grace is greater than it.
The burning bush was never the miracle.
The miracle was that God still chose Moses.
And He still chooses people like us.
From scandal to grace, every excuse surrendered becomes another place where Jesus rewrites everything.
